analysis.one_liner: Makes COVID-19 liability waivers unenforceable at large indoor gatherings where cases are rising.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or vote, so event operators could still require attendees to sign away their right to sue over COVID-19.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would void any agreement making attendees or workers give up their right to sue over catching COVID-19 at an indoor event with more than 1,000 people, in any locality where cases were rising over 14 days. It was introduced in June 2020, referred to the House Judiciary Committee, and never received a hearing or a vote before the term ended.
analysis.who_benefits: People attending or working at large indoor events — concerts, sports games, conventions — in areas with rising COVID-19 cases. If they caught the virus at the event, they would keep the right to sue even if they had signed a waiver, and the bill's placement in federal arbitration law would keep venues from forcing such claims into private arbitration.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Attendees and staff at large indoor events

how_it_helps.text: Anyone who signed a COVID-19 liability waiver to enter an indoor event with more than 1,000 people could still sue if they caught the virus, whenever the event took place in a locality seeing a 14-day rise in cases.
The ban was written into the federal Arbitration Act and states it overrides any other provision there, so venues could not route around it by forcing attendees into arbitration over COVID-19 claims.
The rule applied automatically based on objective conditions — crowd size and local case trends — rather than leaving each attendee to negotiate, which most cannot do with a ticket purchase.

analysis.who_pays: Venues, promoters, and event organizers running large indoor gatherings in rising-case areas would face lawsuits from attendees who caught COVID-19, and their insurers would bear the claims. Some events might be canceled rather than risk the exposure.

drawbacks.text: Venues already devastated by pandemic shutdowns would face open-ended lawsuits, since someone infected days later could try to tie the illness to an event; proving where an infection happened is difficult and would generate disputes.
The bill is a blunt federal override of state contract law, covering only gatherings above 1,000 people indoors — a packed 900-person show or an outdoor superspreader event would get no protection.
Faced with liability they could not waive, some operators would simply cancel events rather than invest in safety measures, costing workers and local businesses their income.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protection is real but narrow: it covers only the largest indoor gatherings in areas with rising cases, and it does nothing about proving that an infection happened at the event. For the people it covers, it removes a take-it-or-leave-it form that most attendees sign without reading. The cost falls on an industry that was already losing money during the pandemic, and some events would likely be canceled instead of held under open liability. It is a targeted fix, not a comprehensive pandemic-liability policy.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Judiciary Committee from June 2020 until the term ended in January 2021 — no hearing, no vote, nothing.

narrative.text: Rep. Mark Pocan introduced the bill on June 18, 2020, during the first wave of states reopening large venues amid the pandemic, with Rep. Mark Takano as the lone cosponsor.
The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced; the committee took no further action on it for the rest of the Congress.
The 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, and the bill died in committee without ever coming to a vote in the full House.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Event venues, promoters, and their insurers came out ahead: they can still require attendees to sign away COVID-19 claims, and no one gained the right to sue that the bill would have created.

for.name: Mark Pocan
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its sole sponsor.

for.name: Mark Takano
for.what_they_did: Original cosponsor — the bill's only cosponsor.

against.name: Jerrold Nadler
against.what_they_did: His committee received the bill on the day it was introduced and never scheduled a hearing or markup, so it never advanced.

against.name: Business and events-industry groups
against.role: Coalition seeking broad COVID-19 liability shields
against.what_they_did: Pushed Congress for broad legal protections for businesses against pandemic lawsuits during 2020, shaping the environment in which this narrow countermeasure received no action.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred; the bill drew two Democratic sponsors, no Republican cosponsors, and no recorded floor opposition.

industries.industry: Live-event venues and promoters (arenas, concert halls, sports and convention operators)
industries.note: The bill would strip their ability to make ticket-buyers and workers sign COVID-19 waivers at large indoor events in rising-case areas, exposing them to lawsuits. Waivers shift the risk of infection onto the person in the cheapest position to avoid it — the attendee — which is why the industry's interest ran against the public's here.
Insurers covering event operators would face claims they currently avoid through enforceable waivers, and could price that exposure into premiums for large indoor events.

industries.industry: Forced-arbitration providers and the arbitration system
industries.note: By writing the ban into the federal Arbitration Act and overriding its other provisions, the bill would keep venues from pushing COVID-19 claims into private arbitration, shrinking one use of that system.
